hook_text: Open an old hand drill and you will find the gear that lets a motor sit sideways. Here is the bevel gear.
clip_script: Spur gears need parallel shafts. Try two at right angles and they catch at a corner and strip. So cut the teeth on a cone instead. Put two cones tip to tip and the teeth meet along a line, and rotation turns a corner, usually 90 degrees. Same ratio rule as always: driven teeth over driver teeth. A 12-tooth bevel driving a 36-tooth bevel turns the corner and gears down three to one. Hand drill: big wheel drives small pinion, bit spins fast. Car axle: small pinion drives big crown wheel, wheels turn slow and strong. In your model, a bevel pair at the drum lets the motor stand where the frame has room. Two rules: the cone tips must meet, and bevels push apart under load, so collar the shafts, or the gears walk out of mesh the moment the cage gets heavy.
visual_style: Two spur gears fail at right angles with a snap; two cones slide tip to tip and mesh; a hand drill section shows crank wheel and pinion; a car axle crown wheel turns; a model drum with a motor standing upright and collars sliding onto the shafts.
pacing: Why spur fails, cones meet, the ratio, drill and car, the model rules.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find one bevel pair in a tool or machine at home.
